items.stem: The exploration is marked out of
items.markingKey: 20. Criteria A–E total 4 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 6.

items.stem: Distinguish between the rationale and the aim.
items.answer: The rationale explains why the topic was chosen; the aim states precisely what the exploration will investigate.
items.markingKey: The rationale explains why the topic was chosen; the aim states precisely what the exploration will investigate. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the topic of an exploration should be of genuine personal interest to the student.
items.answer: Personal interest drives independent thinking, creativity and ownership, which are rewarded under personal engagement, and sustains the effort needed to explore the mathematics in depth.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Personal interest drives independent thinking, creativity and ownership, which are rewarded under personal engagement, and sustains the effort needed to explore the mathematics in depth. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: An exploration is planned on population of a city. Suggest relevant mathematics and state a precise aim that could be answered in 12 to 20 pages.
items.answer: (a) exponential and logistic models, regression, residuals (b) To compare exponential and logistic models for a city's population and assess their predictions
items.markingKey: Relevant mathematics commensurate with the course: exponential and logistic models, regression, residuals (A1 A1); focused, answerable aim (A1); the aim links to the mathematics identified (R1).

items.stem: Ana writes: "The more different topics I include, the higher my mark for use of mathematics." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Criterion E rewards relevant, correct mathematics commensurate with the course and demonstrated understanding, not the number of topics.
items.markingKey: Criterion E rewards relevant, correct mathematics commensurate with the course and demonstrated understanding, not the number of topics. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Using real data always makes an exploration better."
items.answer: Real data helps only when it supports a clear mathematical aim; it is not required.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: real data can show personal engagement; allows modelling and critical reflection. Arguments against: data collection can take over the exploration; pure mathematical topics can score full marks. Supported judgement: Real data helps only when it supports a clear mathematical aim; it is not required.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "scope"?
options: The extent of the investigation: narrow enough to be explored in depth within 12 to 20 pages, broad enough to use mathematics commensurate with the course
Assesses the organisation and coherence of the exploration: a clear introduction, aim, development and conclusion, and conciseness (maximum 4 marks)
A statement believed to be true on the basis of evidence, such as a pattern in calculated cases, but not yet proved
The internal assessment: a written piece of 12 to 20 pages in which a student investigates an area of mathematics of their own choosing
items.answer: The extent of the investigation: narrow enough to be explored in depth within 12 to 20 pages, broad enough to use mathematics commensurate with the course
items.markingKey: A. "scope" is the extent of the investigation: narrow enough to be explored in depth within 12 to 20 pages, broad enough to use mathematics commensurate with the course.

items.stem: Define the term "scope".
items.answer: The extent of the investigation: narrow enough to be explored in depth within 12 to 20 pages, broad enough to use mathematics commensurate with the course
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the extent of the investigation: narrow enough to be explored in depth within 12 to 20 pages, broad enough to use mathematics commensurate with the course. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student proposes the exploration aim: "To learn about complex numbers". Explain why this aim is unsuitable and suggest an improved aim.
items.answer: Unsuitable: a learning goal, not an investigation with a clear outcome. Better: to use complex numbers to find the coordinates of the vertices of regular polygons inscribed in a circle.
items.markingKey: Identifies the weakness: a learning goal, not an investigation with a clear outcome (R1); explains the effect on the assessment criteria, e.g. use of mathematics or reflection (R1); a focused, mathematical alternative such as "to use complex numbers to find the coordinates of the vertices of regular polygons inscribed in a circle" (A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "My aim is to explore everything about the Fibonacci sequence." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: This is far too broad: choose a specific question, e.g. investigating the limit of the ratio of consecutive terms and proving it equals the golden ratio.
items.markingKey: This is far too broad: choose a specific question, e.g. investigating the limit of the ratio of consecutive terms and proving it equals the golden ratio. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Tomás writes in their proposal: "My aim is to show that mathematics is used in sport." Comment on the suitability of this aim and suggest a better one.
items.answer: Unsuitable: vague, with no clear question that can be answered. Better: to model the optimal angle for a long-jump take-off using projectile motion and calculus.
items.markingKey: Identifies the weakness: vague, with no clear question that can be answered (R1); explains the effect on the assessment criteria, e.g. use of mathematics or reflection (R1); a focused, mathematical alternative such as "to model the optimal angle for a long-jump take-off using projectile motion and calculus" (A1).

items.stem: A student plans an exploration with the aim "to find how many perfect riffle shuffles return a deck of n cards to its original order". Explain how the risk of the mathematics becoming too advanced to explain could affect this exploration, and how the student could reduce it.
items.answer: Risk: the mathematics becoming too advanced to explain; mitigation: restrict the aim to a case that can be fully understood and justified
items.markingKey: A risk specific to card shuffling (A1); explanation of its impact on the criteria (R1); a realistic mitigation: restrict the aim to a case that can be fully understood and justified (A1).

items.stem: A student plans an exploration with the aim "to model the profile of a glass with a polynomial and calculate its volume". Explain how the risk of the page limit being exceeded could affect this exploration, and how the student could reduce it.
items.answer: Risk: the page limit being exceeded; mitigation: remove repetitive calculations to an appendix or summarise them in a table
items.markingKey: A risk specific to the shape of a wine glass (A1); explanation of its impact on the criteria (R1); a realistic mitigation: remove repetitive calculations to an appendix or summarise them in a table (A1).

items.stem: An exploration is planned on medicine dosage. Suggest relevant mathematics and state a precise aim that could be answered in 12 to 20 pages.
items.answer: (a) geometric series, exponential decay, limits (b) To model the long-term amount of a drug in the body under repeated doses
items.markingKey: Relevant mathematics commensurate with the course: geometric series, exponential decay, limits (A1 A1); focused, answerable aim (A1); the aim links to the mathematics identified (R1).

items.stem: A student plans an exploration with the aim "to model the number of shares of a post with a logistic model and estimate its carrying capacity". Explain how the risk of the page limit being exceeded could affect this exploration, and how the student could reduce it.
items.answer: Risk: the page limit being exceeded; mitigation: remove repetitive calculations to an appendix or summarise them in a table
items.markingKey: A risk specific to the spread of a rumour on social media (A1); explanation of its impact on the criteria (R1); a realistic mitigation: remove repetitive calculations to an appendix or summarise them in a table (A1).

items.stem:
A student is planning a mathematical exploration about a satellite dish.
(a) Write a precise aim for the exploration.
(b) Identify the mathematics that will be used and explain why it is appropriate.
(c) Describe how personal engagement could be demonstrated.
(d) Explain how reflection could be shown throughout the exploration.
(e) Suggest how technology could be used appropriately.
items.answer: (a) To prove the reflective property of a parabola and find the focus of a real dish (b) conics, the reflective property of a parabola, calculus (c) own data, own questions, own approach, links to personal interest (d) comment on results, limitations of the model, the meaning of the mathematics and possible extensions (e) GDC/GeoGebra/spreadsheet for regression, graphs or iteration, with results interpreted
items.markingKey: (a) focused, answerable (A1 A1) (b) relevant mathematics (A1); justification (R1) (c) R1 R1 (d) R1 R1 (e) A1 [Total 9 marks]

items.stem: "A student should choose an exploration topic that uses the most advanced mathematics possible." Discuss.
items.answer: The mathematics should be commensurate with the course and genuinely understood; ambition is valuable only if the student can use and explain it correctly.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: sophisticated mathematics can score highly in criterion E; shows ambition and engagement. Arguments against: mathematics beyond the student's understanding cannot be explained clearly; communication and reflection may suffer. Supported judgement: The mathematics should be commensurate with the course and genuinely understood; ambition is valuable only if the student can use and explain it correctly. Markbands (6 marks): Criterion-referenced: clear mathematical reasoning, correct notation, a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Criterion C: personal engagement"?
options: A single case that shows a general statement is false
Assesses the extent to which the student engages with the exploration and makes it their own, e.g. independent thinking, creativity, own questions (maximum 3 marks)
The explanation at the start of an exploration of why the topic was chosen and why it is of personal interest
Assesses the use of appropriate mathematical language, notation, symbols, terminology, multiple forms of representation and correctly defined key terms (maximum 4 marks)
items.answer: Assesses the extent to which the student engages with the exploration and makes it their own, e.g. independent thinking, creativity, own questions (maximum 3 marks)
items.markingKey: B. "Criterion C: personal engagement" is assesses the extent to which the student engages with the exploration and makes it their own, e.g. independent thinking, creativity, own questions (maximum 3 marks).

items.stem: An exploration discusses the limitations of the model and the effect of assumptions. Identify the criterion most affected and explain why this would be credited.
items.answer: Criterion D (Reflection)
items.markingKey: Criterion D: Reflection (A1); link the feature to the descriptor for this criterion (R1); justification of why it meets a high band (R1).

items.stem: Kwame writes: "Personal engagement is shown by saying how much I enjoyed the topic." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Statements of interest alone earn little; engagement is shown through independent thinking, own questions, own data and creative approaches.
items.markingKey: Statements of interest alone earn little; engagement is shown through independent thinking, own questions, own data and creative approaches. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: An HL student's exploration is awarded: A 2, B 3, C 1, D 3, E 4. (a) Find the total mark. (b) The exploration is worth 20% of the final assessment; find the percentage of the overall course mark gained. (c) Identify the criterion in which the student achieved the lowest proportion of the available marks.
items.answer: (a) 13/20 (b) 13.0% (c) C (Personal engagement): 1/3
items.markingKey: (a) 2 + 3 + 1 + 3 + 4 = 13 (A1). (b) 13/20 × 20 (M1) = 13.0% (A1). (c) compare mark/maximum for each criterion (M1); C with 1/3 (A1).

items.stem: A teacher reads the following comment about criterion E (use of mathematics): "The mathematics is relevant and mostly correct, at the level of the course, with some understanding demonstrated." Suggest the mark out of 6 and give a reason.
items.answer: 3/6: relevant, partially correct, some understanding
items.markingKey: Mark 3 (±1 accepted with justification) (A1); justification linked to the descriptor: relevant, partially correct, some understanding (R1 R1).

items.stem: An HL student's exploration is awarded: A 4, B 1, C 3, D 0, E 5. (a) Find the total mark. (b) The exploration is worth 20% of the final assessment; find the percentage of the overall course mark gained. (c) Identify the criterion in which the student achieved the lowest proportion of the available marks.
items.markingKey: (a) 4 + 1 + 3 + 0 + 5 = 13 (A1). (b) 13/20 × 20 (M1) = 13.0% (A1). (c) compare mark/maximum for each criterion (M1); D with 0/3 (A1).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Use of mathematics is the only criterion that really matters in the exploration."
items.answer: E is the largest single criterion, but 70% of the marks reward presentation, communication, engagement and reflection, so all criteria matter.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: E carries the most marks (6 of 20); mathematics is the purpose of the exploration. Arguments against: A–D carry 14 of the 20 marks; poor communication can hide good mathematics. Supported judgement: E is the largest single criterion, but 70% of the marks reward presentation, communication, engagement and reflection, so all criteria matter.

items.stem:
A teacher summarises an exploration as follows. A: The exploration has an introduction and conclusion, but the middle sections jump between ideas and some calculations are repeated several times. B: Mathematical language is precise throughout, multiple representations are used appropriately and all key terms are defined. C: The student collects their own data and asks their own questions, but the approach closely follows a published example. D: Limitations of the model are discussed after each stage, and results are linked back to the aim and to possible extensions. E: The mathematics is mostly correct and relevant but contains a significant error in an integral, and understanding is only partly shown.
(a) Suggest a mark for criterion A (presentation), out of 4, and justify it.
(b) Suggest a mark for criterion B (mathematical communication), out of 4, and justify it.
(c) Suggest a mark for criterion C (personal engagement), out of 3, and justify it.
(d) Suggest a mark for criterion D (reflection), out of 3, and justify it.
(e) Suggest a mark for criterion E (use of mathematics), out of 6, and justify it.
(f) Find the total mark for the exploration based on your suggested marks.
(g) Recommend, with a reason, the single change that would most improve the mark.
items.answer: (a) 2/4: some coherence but not well organised or concise (b) 4/4: consistently appropriate and precise communication (c) 2/3: significant but not outstanding engagement (d) 3/3: substantial, critical reflection throughout (e) 2/6: relevant mathematics with significant errors (f) 13/20 (g) improve criterion E (use of mathematics), where the lowest proportion of marks was gained
items.markingKey: (a) A1 R1 (b) A1 R1 (c) A1 R1 (d) A1 R1 (e) A1 R1 (f) A1 (g) identify lowest proportion (R1); specific improvement (R1) [Total 13 marks]

items.answer: Criterion D: reflection
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of Criterion D: reflection.

items.stem: Explain why "meaningful reflection" requires more than a concluding paragraph.
items.answer: Reflection is credited when the student critically examines results throughout — linking them to the aim, considering limitations, accuracy and implications — not when a brief summary is added at the end.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Reflection is credited when the student critically examines results throughout — linking them to the aim, considering limitations, accuracy and implications — not when a brief summary is added at the end. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between Criterion D: reflection and Criterion C: personal engagement.
items.answer: C rewards making the exploration one's own (independent thinking, creativity); D rewards critically reviewing and evaluating results and the process.
items.markingKey: C rewards making the exploration one's own (independent thinking, creativity); D rewards critically reviewing and evaluating results and the process. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: For Sₙ = 1 + 5 + 5² + … + 5ⁿ⁻¹, the first four values are 1, 6, 31, 156. Which formula fits?

A student checks that Sₙ = n(n + 1)(n + 2)/3 for Sₙ = 1×2 + 2×3 + … + n(n + 1) is correct for n = 1, 2, …, 5 and claims this proves it. Explain why this is not a proof and outline how the result could be proved.
items.answer: checking finitely many cases is not a proof; use induction
items.markingKey: Finitely many cases do not establish the result for all n (R1); base case n = 1 (M1); inductive step: k(k + 1)(k + 2)/3 + (k + 1)(k + 2) = (k + 1)(k + 2)(k + 3)/3 (R1).

items.stem: Maya writes: "Since the formula works for n = 1, 2 and 3 it is true for all positive integers." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Checking cases is evidence, not proof; a general argument such as induction is required.
items.markingKey: Checking cases is evidence, not proof; a general argument such as induction is required. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Consider Sₙ = 1×2 + 2×2² + … + n×2ⁿ. (a) Find the values for n = 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. (b) Conjecture a formula in terms of n. (c) Use your formula to find the value when n = 20.
items.markingKey: (a) values (A1 A1). (b) pattern recognised (M1); Sₙ = (n − 1)2ⁿ⁺¹ + 2 (A1). (c) substitute n = 20 (M1); 39845890 (A1).

items.markingKey: The direction is reversed: assume P(k) and deduce P(k + 1). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the pattern 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 for the number of regions in a circle does not prove that the number of regions is 2ⁿ⁻¹.
items.answer: Finitely many cases cannot establish a general rule; in fact the sixth value is 31, not 32, so the conjecture is false.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Paper 3 questions often ask you to test a conjecture on further cases before proving it.
items.answer: Testing builds confidence and can reveal a counterexample early; it also suggests the structure that the general proof must follow.

This question explores the "prime-generating" polynomial n² − n + 17.
(a) Find f(n) = n² − n + 17 for n = 1, …, 5 and verify that each value is prime.
